articleTitle: An approach to combined cycle distributed control and data transmission
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Control Systems for Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
abstract: The combined cycle power plant consists of three major components: the gas turbine generator (GTG), the heat recovery steam generator (HRSG), and the steam turbine generator (STG). Each of these components may be arranged in various configurations depending on the power output, flexibility and availability required from the power plant. In many cases each major component may be supplied by different manufacturers. Alternatively the power plant user or supplier may standardise on the major plant items but want to maintain competition between control system suppliers. The author discusses the advantages of an integrated distributed control system and examines how plant wide data can be handled by the distributed control system data highway in a fast, predictable and secure manner. The presentation of the data is discussed with the objective of simplifying the operators tasks and providing plant managers with information to obtain optimal performance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Commercial control of gas turbine combined cycle generators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Control Systems for Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
abstract: Control systems for combined cycle gas turbines perform a number of functions which may be related to questions of safety, machine condition, plant performance or commercial operations. The authors discuss the latter and in particular the system of operational control which may be required in meeting the requirements of the Pooling and Settlement Agreement (P and SA) within the Grid Code. Output of electricity into the distribution and transmission system in excess of 10 Mw must be sold through the P and SA. Any generator which has an export capacity of 100 MW or above is subject to central despatch by the National Grid controller. It can be expected therefore that the sale of the electrical output of combined cycle gas turbine generators will be subject to the rules of the P and SA and that their operation will be subject to the requirements of the grid code. The authors describe the impact of the P and SA and the Grid Code on the commercial operation of a combined cycle gas turbine generator and the control systems, in their widest sense, which can be employed to meet commercial goals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A user's experience in the control and operation of combined cycle power plants
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Control Systems for Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
abstract: The Irish Electricity Supply Board's operational experience with combined cycle power plants began early in 1979 at Marina, Cork. The plant comprises an 85 MW Frame 9001B gas turbine repowering a 1954 Siemens 30 MW steam turbine using a CMI unfired heat recovery boiler. Excellent performance of the Marina plant prompted the installation of a further plant at North Wall, Dublin in 1982. The North Wall plant consists of a 104 MW Frame 9001E gas turbine repowering three 16 MW BBC steam turbines (also of 1950s vintage), using a similar CMI boiler. The authors outline practical experience of the control and operation of these plants.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control systems in large combined cycle power stations
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Control Systems for Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
abstract: The concept of a centralised control room is readily accepted as an essential requirement for running modern power plant. The operator is provided with all the necessary plant information and controls to run the station from a logically laid out desk. Modern control schemes offer flexible control and automation along with the ability to handle and present large amounts of information within very short response times. However, all systems have their limitations and care must still be taken when applying such technology. The GEC ALSTHOM group has built up the necessary expertise over many years, both on high reliability design and project management of large turn key power plant projects. This ensures a totally integrated power plant package is provided. Mainly using the example of GEC ALSTHOM's standard Vega 209f design the author explains the philosophy used in selecting control and instrumentation for a large combined cycle power plant.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
